overview: Tenacity 6.0's LongJump is a six-mode movement booster that combines three axes of abuse: a client tick-rate multiplier through Timer.timerSpeed (10x, 30x or 50x depending on the mode), a vertical motionY boost of 0.4 to 4.0, and a horizontal speed write through MovementUtil.setSpeed of 1.2 to 9.6 blocks per tick. The Verus and Vulcan modes first damage themselves with their own fireball (the hotbar scan finds item.fireball or item.firecharge and sendUseItem throws it at the player's feet), so the burst rides real server-granted explosion velocity from S12 before the module adds its own speed; the Fireball mode is the trigger-only version, waiting for an external hurtTime of at least 7 before writing speed 1.2. The Grim mode is the crudest: timer 50x, motionY 0.4 and speed 9 in a single pre-motion pass, then it toggles off. Several state fields (jumps, stage, damageStage, firstVelocity, velocityMotionY and the jumpPackets list) are reset in onEnable but never read anywhere in the file, dead state left from a removed mode.

sections.p: One MotionEvent consumer dispatches the six modes. Mineland applies a 0.1 speed and toggles; NCP waits for hurtTime above 0 and writes motionY 0.5; Fireball waits for hurtTime at least 7 and writes speed 1.2; Verus Fast and High run the fireball self-hit then, on hurtTime above 0, write motionY 1.0 or 4.0 with timerSpeed 10 or 30 and speed 9.6 or 9; Vulcan runs the fireball self-hit, then on hurtTime above 8 sets timerSpeed 0.1 with motionY 4.0 and speed 2.6; Grim writes motionY 0.4 with timerSpeed 50 and speed 9 on the first pre-motion pass. Every mode toggles the module off immediately after its boost, so each use is a single-shot burst.

Timer.timerSpeed multiplies the client's tick rate. At 10x the client runs 200 ticks per second and emits roughly 200 C03 packets per second instead of 20; at 30x and 50x that becomes 600 and 1000 packets per second. The burst lasts only one or two ticks of module time, but a single boosted tick already produces 10 to 50 movement packets, which is the entire wire signature the rate checks read. The Vulcan mode inverts the axis: timerSpeed 0.1 slows the client to 2 ticks per second, so its 2.6 speed moves arrive as huge per-packet deltas instead of a packet flood.

The Verus and Vulcan modes first throw a fireball from the hotbar with sendUseItem, which sends C08 use-item and lets the explosion damage the player, setting hurtTime and granting real S12 explosion velocity. The module then adds motionY 1.0 to 4.0 and horizontal speed 9 to 9.6 on top of the legitimate knockback, so the burst is a mix of server-granted velocity and client-written motion. The NCP and Grim modes skip the self-hit and write the vertical boost directly, which is the profile the vertical movement checks reject outright.

files.label: LongJumpModule.java (module)
files.explanation:
The module is the full exploit. The MotionEvent consumer branches on the mode string and, in the Verus mode, on the Type sub-setting, and every branch writes one or more of Timer.timerSpeed, mc.thePlayer.motionY and MovementUtil.setSpeed, then calls toggle() to disarm after the single boost. The fireball scan walks the hotbar for item.fireball or item.firecharge and calls sendUseItem, which is the self-damage step that arms the hurtTime gate and produces the server-granted explosion velocity.

onEnable restores the tick-rate multiplier to 1 and clears the state fields, and onDisable restores both timer fields. The declared state (jumps, stage, damageStage, firstVelocity, velocityMotionY and the jumpPackets list) is written in onEnable and never read anywhere in the file, so those resets are the only trace of a removed mode.

files.label: MovementUtil.java (speed write)
files.explanation:
MovementUtil.setSpeed is the horizontal velocity writer every mode calls. It derives the movement yaw from the input state (getDirection, with the 180-degree flip for backward input and the strafe adjustments), and writes motionX and motionZ as the sine and cosine of that yaw scaled by the requested speed, bailing out when the player is not pressing any movement key. The single-argument form used by LongJump replaces the horizontal motion entirely rather than adding to it, which is why the boost is a hard speed pin instead of an acceleration.

The same class carries getSpeed, getAllowedHDistNCP (the NCP-style horizontal allowance helper) and the strafe-percentage variant, but the LongJump module only touches setSpeed and getDirection.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (horizontal and vertical envelope)
countering.explanation:
SurvivalFly's horizontal allowance comes from prepareSpeedEstimation, which predicts the per-tick sprint distance (0.91 air inertia with the sprint boost) and measures the reported move against it; the violation is (max(hDistanceAboveLimit, 0.0) + max(yDistanceAboveLimit, 0.0)) * 100 with a set-back to the stored location. The module's speed writes of 2.6 to 9.6 blocks per tick sit far above the predicted 0.31 to 0.62, so hDistanceAboveLimit lands near the write value minus the prediction and the violation reaches hundreds to nearly a thousand on the first boosted move, followed by a set-back.

The vertical half catches the motionY writes: the jump envelope (LiftOffEnvelope, jump gain 0.42 with a 10-tick jumpDelay window) tolerates the launch itself, but the NCP and Grim modes write 0.5 and 0.4 at arbitrary air ticks and the Verus High mode writes 4.0, which exceeds the gain several times over and produces a yDistanceAboveLimit of several blocks on the same move that already failed horizontally.

countering.label: MorePackets (movement packet rate)
countering.explanation:
MorePackets counts the raw rate of serverbound movement packets, content-blind. Every processed C03 is scored into data.morePacketsFreq, an ActionFrequency with 500ms buckets, and NetStatic.morePacketsCheck accumulates the window score against cc.morePacketsEPSMax, default 22 packets per second with 20 ideal, plus a burst path on the newest half-second bucket (default 15 packets) with lag adaption via TickTask. A violation returns the morePacketsSetBack location seeded from the SurvivalFly set-back.

The timer multipliers are a direct hit. At timerSpeed 10 the client emits about 200 packets per second, at 30 about 600, and at 50 about 1000, so a single boosted tick already exceeds the 22 per second ceiling and the 15 packet half-second burst limit, and the violation fires on the same tick the boost lands. The Vulcan mode's slowdown produces the opposite profile, fewer packets, which this check never sees, but its 2.6 speed moves fail SurvivalFly anyway.

countering.label: TickRate (clock-drift tick rate)
countering.explanation:
Hawk's TickRate enforces the client tick rate through a clock-drift accumulator. Each move event adds (elapsed nanos minus 50ms) to the player's drift, and when the drift passes the clockDriftThresholdMillis of -50ms (the client clock is ahead, meaning packets arrive faster than 20 per second) the check punishes and rubber-bands, with the drift clamped back to the threshold. Positive drift from lag is absorbed by MAX_CATCHUP_TIME of 2000ms. The javadoc states the check can detect at least a 3% increase in tick-rate frequency almost immediately.

Every timer-boosted packet arrives roughly 5ms apart at timerSpeed 10 (1ms at 50), so each one adds about -45 to -49ms of drift, and the -50ms threshold crosses after one or two packets, producing an instant punish and rubber-band on the boost tick. The honest boundary is the Vulcan mode's 0.1x slowdown: its 500ms packet gaps add positive drift that the 2000ms catch-up cap absorbs, so the slow-timer half of the module is invisible to this check.

countering.label: Speed (stage table and hard cap)
countering.explanation:
Arc v2's Speed check models expected horizontal speed per stage. Off ground the expectation is the base 0.2873 (scaled by speed potions) plus a stage adder of 0.049 when the vertical is zero, 0.08 when descending under 0.34, or 0.3261 when rising at or above 0.34, and the check hard-fails any move above 8 blocks in a single tick. On the ground, once groundTicks reaches 5, the expected value is thisMove divided by groundTime plus the base, with the jumping-while-grounded case adding vertical over thisMove.

The module's 9 to 9.6 speed writes trip the hard gate: 9.6 is above 8, so check() returns true immediately with no tolerance, and even the Vulcan mode's 2.6 is four to five times the off-ground expectation, producing the BunnyHop violation and the previous-location setback. The fireball velocity does not excuse the excess because the check consumes the velocity vector through getRecentVelocity(ping) and adds its length to the expectation, so only the server-granted portion is forgiven.
